implementation_notes: Swift's sprawl usually appears on the backend, where Vapor or Hummingbird make a small service per resource easy, and on the client side as an app that talks to dozens of its own services. The cost is the general one, plus something iOS-specific worth naming: a mobile client that must discover and contact many services cannot be tested against a local environment that mirrors the fleet. The consolidation on the backend is one Vapor application with several route groups, which keeps the resource boundaries explicit and removes the deployment boundaries. Apple's own frameworks are examples of the opposite extreme — a single service with a huge surface — so the scale that suits is genuinely a judgement.
idiom_name: one microservice per resource; server-side Swift service per noun
pitfalls: A mobile client cannot mirror a fleet locally, so integration testing requires a deployed environment with N services.
Server-side Swift services inherit the JVM-free but memory-heavy profile of Swift runtimes per service.
Resource-per-service decomposition is the same bounded-context confusion as in every other stack, expressed as REST paths.
